title: INT 21h, fifteen DOS file and device calls
covers: INT 21h, the DOS services the pilot writes: file calls and IOCTL subfunctions.

rows.text: Terminate program, a DOS 1 call.
CS holds the PSP segment.
Microsoft recommends INT 21h AH=4Ch for DOS 2 and later.
The program's return code (ERRORLEVEL) is set to 00h.
Execution continues at the address stored in INT 22 after DOS performs whatever cleanup it needs.
The cleanup restores INT 22, INT 23 and INT 24 from the PSP assumed at offset 0000h of the segment the stack copy of CS gives.
If the PSP is its own parent, the process's memory is not freed.
If the PSP is its own parent and INT 22 also points into the terminating program, the process is effectively not terminated.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x00.
With SP above 0xFFFA the CS is popped off the stack; with DOS 7 or later, long names and certain stack words, the current PSP is terminated instead.
After the terminate call it throws int 9000 when a Ctrl+C INT 23 is in progress.
It clears the flag that a DOS program is running and empties the stored program name and arguments.
Read a character from standard input, with echo, a DOS 1 call.
AL holds the character read.
^C and ^Break are checked, and INT 23 is executed if one is read.
^P toggles the DOS-internal echo-to-printer flag.
^Z is not interpreted, so it does not cause an EOF if input is redirected.
The character is echoed to standard output.
Under DOS 1.x standard input is always the keyboard and standard output the screen.
Under DOS 2 and later standard input and standard output may be redirected.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x01.
Standard input is read through the STDIN handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
With DOS major version 1 reported it sets dos.echo before the read and clears it after the read.
Write a character to standard output, a DOS 1 call.
DL holds the character to write.
AL holds the last character output, although the official documents state nothing is returned (at least DOS 2.1 to 7.0).
AL is the character in DL, except that DL=09h gives AL=20h as tabs are expanded to blanks.
^C and ^Break are checked, and INT 23 is executed if pressed.
Under DOS 1.x standard output is always the screen.
Under DOS 2 and later standard output may be redirected.
If standard output is redirected to a file, no error checks (write-protected, full media, etc.) are performed.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x02.
Output is written through the STDOUT handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
Read a character from STDAUX, a DOS 1 call.
AL holds the character read.
The keyboard is checked for ^C and ^Break, and INT 23 is executed if one is detected.
STDAUX is usually the first serial port.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x03.
STDAUX is read through serialports[0] into AL, but with the word at 0x40:0x00 zero, or that port object missing, nothing is read and AL is left as it was.
Before reading it writes 0x03 to the port at base plus 4, commented RTS/DTR on, the base being the word at 0x40:0x00.
Write a character to STDAUX, a DOS 1 call.
DL holds the character to write.
The keyboard is checked for ^C and ^Break, and INT 23 is executed if one is detected.
STDAUX is usually the first serial port.
If STDAUX is busy, the call waits until it becomes free.
Nothing is returned: the list gives this call no Return line.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x04.
STDAUX is written through serialports[0] from DL, but with the word at 0x40:0x00 zero, or that port object missing, the character is dropped.
Around the write it sets the port at base plus 4 to 0x03 (RTS/DTR on) before and to 0x01 (RTS off) after.
Write a character to the printer, a DOS 1 call.
DL holds the character to print.
The keyboard is checked for ^C and ^Break, and INT 23 is executed if one is detected.
STDPRN is usually the first parallel port, but may be redirected under DOS 2 and later.
If the printer is busy, the call waits.
Nothing is returned: the list gives this call no Return line.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x05.
The character goes to the first existing of three parallel port objects, not through the STDPRN handle, and is dropped if none exists.
Direct console output, a DOS 1 call, when DL is not FFh.
DL holds the character to write.
AL holds the character output, although the official docs state nothing is returned (at least DOS 2.1 to 7.0).
^C and ^Break are not checked.
Under DOS 1.x standard output is always the screen.
Under DOS 2 and later standard output may be redirected.
With DL=FFh the call is direct console input.
ZF is set if no character is available.
AL is 00h if no character is available, although this is not documented and some programs rely on it.
ZF is clear if a character is available.
AL holds the character read if one is available.
^C and ^Break are not checked on input.
A returned character of 00h means an extended keycode, which the next call of this function returns.
Under DOS 1.x standard input is always the keyboard.
Under DOS 2 and later standard input may be redirected.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x06, and DL=0xFF selects the input branch.
Output is written through the STDOUT handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
It sets dos.direct_output true around the write and false after it.
Input is read through the STDIN handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
Before polling input it calls overhead, which adds 2 to the guest IP register.
Direct character input without echo, a DOS 1 call.
AL holds the character read from standard input.
^C and ^Break are not checked.
Under DOS 1.x standard input is always the keyboard.
Under DOS 2 and later standard input may be redirected.
If the interim console flag is set (see AX=6301h), partially-formed double-byte characters may be returned.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x07.
Input is read through the STDIN handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
Character input without echo, a DOS 1 call.
AL holds the character read from standard input.
^C and ^Break are checked, and INT 23 is executed if one is detected.
Under DOS 1.x standard input is always the keyboard.
Under DOS 2 and later standard input may be redirected.
If the interim console flag is set (see AX=6301h), partially-formed double-byte characters may be returned.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x08.
A ^C read runs the break action and test, but from a redirected regular file the ^C is then skipped and the next character is read.
Input is read through the STDIN handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
When the read fails or returns no bytes the loop ends with AL set to 0.
Write a string to standard output, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to a '$'-terminated string.
The '$'-terminated string is written to standard output.
AL holds 24h, the '$' ending the string, although the official docs state nothing is returned (at least DOS 2.1 to 7.0 and NWDOS).
^C and ^Break are checked, and INT 23 is called if either is pressed.
Under DOS 1.x standard output is always the screen.
Under DOS 2 and later standard output may be redirected.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x09.
The string is written through STDOUT, except a Windows-only program's 'cannot be run in DOS mode' message when winautorun, quiet start are on and secure mode is off.
Output is written through the STDOUT handle at any reported DOS version, the DOS 1 case included.
Buffered input, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to the input buffer.
The buffer is filled with user input.
^C and ^Break are checked, and INT 23 is called if either is detected.
Input is read from standard input, which may be redirected under DOS 2 and later.
If the maximum buffer size is 00h the call returns immediately without reading any input.
Byte 00h of the buffer holds the maximum number of characters it can hold.
On call, byte 01h holds the number of characters from the last input which may be recalled.
On return, byte 01h holds the number of characters actually read, excluding the CR.
From offset 02h the buffer holds the characters read, including the final carriage return.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x0a.
Byte 01h receives, at the end, a local counter that starts at 0 and is raised after each character stored in the buffer.
When the read returns no bytes, the emulator ends with the error message about redirected input reaching EOF.
A line feed (10) read is skipped.
A backspace scans the buffered characters, flagging double-byte characters and, on a JEGA or DOS/V display, hat characters.
A backspace then erases the last character by writing BS, space, BS to standard output, doubled for a two-cell character, and lowers the count by one or two.
With a JEGA or DOS/V display a bell character (7) is written to standard output and is not stored in the buffer.
When the buffer is full a character other than CR is refused: a bell is written and the cursor is put back if the bell moved it.
Each accepted character is also written to standard output as it is stored.
Get the standard input status, a DOS 1 call.
AL is 00h if no character is available.
AL is FFh if a character is available.
^C and ^Break are checked, and INT 23 is called if either is pressed.
Under DOS 1.x standard input is always the keyboard.
Under DOS 2 and later standard input may be redirected.
If the interim console flag is set (see AX=6301h), AL is FFh when a partially-formed double-byte character is available.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x0b, and the status comes from DOS_GetSTDINStatus.
The status is read from the STDIN handle at any reported DOS version.
The case body holds no interim console flag test.
DOS_GetSTDINStatus holds no interim console flag test.
After setting AL the call runs overhead, which adds 2 to the guest IP register.
Flush the input buffer and read standard input, a DOS 1 call.
AL holds the standard input function to execute after flushing the buffer.
Other registers are set as the chosen input function needs.
The registers returned are those the specified input function returns.
If AL is not one of 01h, 06h, 07h, 08h or 0Ah, no input is attempted.
The input buffer is flushed, and also when AL is not one of those functions.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x0c.
The buffer is flushed only when the STDIN handle is the CON device, by reading and dropping characters while the status says one is available.
For an AL that selects no input function the call sets AL to 0.
After the input function runs the call restores the caller's AH.
Flush the input buffer, then run the standard input function AL selects (01h).
AL=01h selects standard input function 01h to run after the flush.
The registers returned are those of the input function AL selects.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by case 0x1 of the switch on AL inside its case 0x0c.
After the input function runs the call restores the caller's AH.
Flush the input buffer, then run the standard input function AL selects (06h).
AL=06h selects standard input function 06h to run after the flush.
The registers returned are those of the input function AL selects.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by case 0x6 of the switch on AL inside its case 0x0c.
After the input function runs the call restores the caller's AH.
Flush the input buffer, then run the standard input function AL selects (07h).
AL=07h selects standard input function 07h to run after the flush.
The registers returned are those of the input function AL selects.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by case 0x7 of the switch on AL inside its case 0x0c.
After the input function runs the call restores the caller's AH.
Flush the input buffer, then run the standard input function AL selects (08h).
AL=08h selects standard input function 08h to run after the flush.
The registers returned are those of the input function AL selects.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by case 0x8 of the switch on AL inside its case 0x0c.
After the input function runs the call restores the caller's AH.
Flush the input buffer, then run the standard input function AL selects (0Ah).
AL=0Ah selects standard input function 0Ah to run after the flush.
The registers returned are those of the input function AL selects.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by case 0xa of the switch on AL inside its case 0x0c.
After the input function runs the call restores the caller's AH.
Disk reset, a DOS 1 call.
In DOS 6, CF is clear on return.
Versions of DOS before 6 preserve CF.
All modified disk buffers are written to disk.
The directory information is not updated: that is only done when files are closed or a SYNC call is issued.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x0d.
CF is not modified, whatever DOS version is reported, DOS 6 included.
The case body writes no disk buffers.
Select the default drive, a DOS 1 call.
DL holds the new default drive: 00h is A:, 01h is B:, and so on.
AL holds the number of potentially valid drive letters.
Under DOS 3.0 and later AL is the greatest of 5, the LASTDRIVE= value in CONFIG.SYS and the number of drives actually present.
On a DOS 1.x or 2.x single-floppy system AL is 2; otherwise AL is the highest drive actually present.
DOS 1.x supports at most 16 drives, DOS 2.x 63, and DOS 3 and later 26.
The parse FCB call (AH=29h) can be used to determine whether a drive letter is valid.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x0e, and DOS_SetDefaultDrive sets the drive.
AL is the larger of maxdrive (1 when outside 1 to 26) and the number of the highest mounted drive, at any reported version.
AL is not forced to 2 on a single-floppy setup; the maxdrive and highest mounted drive rule applies at any reported version.
The scan runs up to DOS_DRIVES at any reported version, so the DOS 1.x and 2.x drive limits are not applied.
With the DOS kernel disabled the call leaves the default drive as it was.
A drive number at or above DOS_DRIVES, or 2 or more with no drive mounted, leaves the default drive as it was.
Open a file using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an unopened File Control Block.
AL is 00h if the open succeeded.
AL is FFh if the file is not found or access is denied.
From DOS 3.1 the file is opened for read/write in compatibility mode.
An unopened FCB has the drive, filename and extension fields filled in and all other bytes cleared.
On a FAT32 drive the call only succeeds for creating a volume label, since FAT32 does not support FCBs for file I/O.
With APPEND of DOS 3.3 and later loaded, DX is corrupted if the file is not found.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x0f, and DOS_FCBOpen opens the file.
A name with a wildcard is first resolved by FCB find first, and the first match is the file opened.
A file already open under the same name is shared: its reference count is raised and the FCB takes its handle.
A failed open calls SetSeqData on the FCB with 0xFF and 0.
DX is left as it was when the open fails.
Close a file using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to the File Control Block.
AL is 00h if the close succeeded.
AL is FFh if the close failed.
A successful close forces all disk buffers used by the file to be written and the directory entry to be updated.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x10, and DOS_FCBClose closes the file.
Find the first matching file using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an unopened FCB, which may contain '?' wildcards.
AL is 00h if a file matched.
If a file matched, the DTA holds an unopened FCB for the first matching file.
AL is FFh if there is no matching filename or the FCB is bad.
The type of the returned FCB depends on whether the input FCB was normal or extended.
The DTA data is the drive number (or extended FCB header and drive number) followed by the file's directory entry, compatible with an unopened FCB.
For an extended FCB with search attribute 08h the volume label, if any, is returned even if the current directory is not the root.
From DOS 3.0 the '*' wildcard is also allowed.
The search FCB must not be modified if AH=12h will be used to continue searching.
DOS 3.3 sets offset 0Dh (directory entry number), 0Fh (current directory cluster), 15h (drive number), and 0Ch and 11h to values the list does not know.
The function is used by many copy protection schemes to obtain the starting cluster of a file.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x11, and DOS_FCBFindFirst searches.
The search runs with the DTA pointed at a private temporary area, and the caller's DTA is restored afterwards.
Find the next matching file using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an unopened FCB.
AL is 00h if a file matched.
If a file matched, the Disk Transfer Area is filled with an unopened FCB.
AL is FFh if there are no more matching filenames.
A successful find first on the search FCB is assumed to have been executed before the call.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x12, and DOS_FCBFindNext searches.
The search runs with the DTA pointed at a private temporary area, and the caller's DTA is restored afterwards.
Delete files using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an unopened FCB whose filename is a template for deletion, '?' wildcards allowed.
AL is 00h if one or more files were deleted.
AL is FFh if no files matched or all were read-only or locked.
From DOS 1.25 an extended FCB with filename '???????????' and attribute bits 0-4 set (bits 1 and 2 for DOS 1.x) deletes everything in the current directory.
In that case the first byte of the name is set to 00h (entry never used) instead of E5h.
This may have originally been an optimization to minimize directory searching after a mass deletion.
It can corrupt the filesystem under DOS 2 and later because subdirectories are removed without deleting the files they contain.
Currently open files should not be deleted.
MS-DOS allows deletion of read-only files with an extended FCB.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x13, and DOS_FCBDeleteFile deletes.
Create or truncate a file using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an unopened FCB; wildcards are not allowed.
AL is 00h if the call succeeded.
AL is FFh if the directory is full or the file exists and is read-only or locked.
If the file already exists it is truncated to zero length.
With an extended FCB the file is given the attribute in the FCB; this is how a volume label is created in the root directory.
On a FAT32 drive the call only succeeds for creating a volume label, since FAT32 does not support FCBs for file I/O.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x16, and DOS_FCBCreate creates the file.
The FCB's attribute is passed on to the create or, with the volume bit, to the drive's FileCreate, but an attribute of 0 becomes archive.
On success the FCB takes the handle of the new file.
Rename files using an FCB, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to a modified FCB.
The old filename ('?' wildcards OK) is in the standard location of the FCB.
The new filename ('?' wildcards OK, no drive) is in the 11 bytes beginning at offset 11h.
AL is 00h if the rename succeeded.
AL is FFh if no files matched, the file is read-only, or the new name already exists.
Subdirectories may be renamed using an extended FCB with the appropriate attribute, as may volume labels.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x17, and DOS_FCBRenameFile renames.
Read sequentially from an FCB file, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an opened FCB.
AL is 00h if the read succeeded.
AL is 01h at end of file, with no data.
AL is 02h for a segment wrap in the DTA.
AL is 03h at end of file when a partial record was read.
The Disk Transfer Area is filled with the record read from the file.
A record of the size specified in the FCB is read beginning at the current file position.
Then the current block and current record fields in the FCB are updated.
If a partial record was read, it is zero-padded to the full size.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x14, and DOS_FCBRead reads the record.
The record is copied by one MEM_BlockWrite to the DTA linear address plus the record number times the record size.
FCB_READ_NODATA is returned when the read gets no bytes, and also when the reopen of a closed FCB, the seek or the read fails.
A handle that is invalid or no longer open makes the call open the FCB again first.
A record size of 0 in the FCB is taken as 128 and stored back.
Write sequentially to an FCB file, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an opened FCB.
The Disk Transfer Area holds the record to be written.
AL is 00h if the write succeeded.
AL is 01h if the disk is full.
AL is 02h for a segment wrap in the DTA.
A record of the size specified in the FCB is written beginning at the current file position.
Then the current block and current record fields in the FCB are updated.
If less than a full sector is written, the data is placed in a DOS buffer to be written out at a later time.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x15, and DOS_FCBWrite writes the record.
FCB_ERR_WRITE is returned when the closed-handle test passes and the reopen fails, or when the seek or the write call fails.
The record is read from the DTA's linear address plus record number times record size, so a record crossing the segment end is read on past it.
The FCB is addressed by DS:DX, and one whose handle is invalid or no longer open is opened again first, instead of being required open.
A record size of 0 in the FCB is taken as 128 and stored back.
The file size in the FCB grows when the write passes its end, and the file date and time are set from the DOS date and the BIOS tick count.
Null function for CP/M compatibility, a DOS 1 call.
AL is 00h.
It corresponds to the CP/M BDOS function "get bit map of logged drives", which is meaningless under MS-DOS.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x18, which jumps to the default label that sets AL to 0.
It logs an error that the call is unhandled when AH is below 0x6B.
Null function for CP/M compatibility, a DOS 1 call.
AL is 00h.
It corresponds to the CP/M BDOS function "get bit map of read-only drives", which is meaningless under MS-DOS.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x1d, which jumps to the default label that sets AL to 0.
It logs an error that the call is unhandled when AH is below 0x6B.
Null function for CP/M compatibility, a DOS 1 call.
AL is 00h.
It corresponds to the CP/M BDOS function "set file attributes", which was meaningless under MS-DOS 1.x.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x1e, which jumps to the default label that sets AL to 0.
It logs an error that the call is unhandled when AH is below 0x6B.
Null function for CP/M compatibility, a DOS 1 call.
AL is 00h.
It corresponds to the CP/M BDOS function "get/set default user (sublibrary) number", which is meaningless under MS-DOS.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x20, which jumps to the default label that sets AL to 0.
It logs an error that the call is unhandled when AH is below 0x6B.
Get the current default drive, a DOS 1 call.
AL is the drive: 00h is A:, 01h is B:, and so on.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x19, and DOS_GetDefaultDrive gives the drive.
A drive in the SDA that differs from the emulator's current drive is logged as an error, and the current drive is the one returned.
Set the Disk Transfer Area address, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to the Disk Transfer Area (DTA).
The DTA is set to PSP:0080h when a program is started.
Nothing is returned: the list gives this call no Return line.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x1a, which sets the DTA from DS:DX.
Get allocation information for the default drive, a DOS 1 call.
AL is the number of sectors per cluster (allocation unit).
CX is the number of bytes per sector.
DX is the total number of clusters.
DS:BX points to the media ID byte.
Under DOS 1.x, DS:BX points at an actual copy of the FAT.
Later versions return a pointer to a copy of the FAT's ID byte.
The function may not be properly supported on CD-ROMs and other installable file systems; AX=4402h is to be used for CD-ROMs instead.
DOS 7.10 (Win95B/Win98) reportedly returns incorrect values in AL and DX for FAT12/FAT16 drives, though correct ones for FAT32; only real-mode DOS is affected, not DOS windows.
The media ID byte is FFh, FEh, FDh, FCh, FAh, F9h, F8h or F0h, by floppy sides and sectors per track, hard disk or other media.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x1b, and DOS_GetAllocationInfo with drive 0, which takes the default drive from DOS_GetDefaultDrive, is given pointers to AL, CX and DX.
DS:BX is set to an entry of the dos.tables.mediaid table, at the drive number times dos.tables.dpb_size.
When the drive number is not below DOS_DRIVES or no drive is mounted there, the DOS error is set to invalid drive and AL is set to 0xFF.
Get allocation information for a specific drive, a DOS 1 call.
DL is the drive: 00h is the default, 01h is A:, and so on.
AL is the number of sectors per cluster (allocation unit).
AL is FFh if the drive is invalid.
CX is the number of bytes per sector.
DX is the total number of clusters.
DS:BX points to the media ID byte.
Under DOS 1.x, DS:BX points at an actual copy of the FAT.
Later versions return a pointer to a copy of the FAT's ID byte.
The function may not be properly supported on CD-ROMs and other installable file systems; AX=4402h is to be used for CD-ROMs instead.
DOS 7.10 (Win95B/Win98) reportedly returns incorrect values in AL and DX for FAT12/FAT16 drives, though correct ones for FAT32; only real-mode DOS is affected, not DOS windows.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x1c, and DOS_GetAllocationInfo takes DL as the drive.
DS:BX is set to an entry of the dos.tables.mediaid table, at the drive number times dos.tables.dpb_size.
Get the drive parameter block for the default drive, a DOS 1 call.
AL is 00h if successful.
On success DS:BX points to the Drive Parameter Block (DPB); see table 01357 for DOS 1.x and AH=32h for DOS 2 and later.
AL is FFh for an invalid drive.
The call was undocumented before DOS 5.0, and only the DOS 4.0 and later version of the DPB has been documented.
The DOS 1.1 and MS-DOS 1.25 DPB starts with the sequential device ID at 00h and the logical drive number, 0 for A:, at 01h.
Then come the bytes per sector at 02h, the highest sector number in a cluster at 04h and the cluster shift count at 05h.
Then 06h is the first FAT sector, 08h the FAT copies, 09h the directory entries, 0Bh the first data sector and 0Dh the highest cluster number.
Then 0Fh is the sectors per FAT, 10h the first directory sector and 12h the address of the allocation table.
The DOS 1.0 table is the same except that the first and last fields are missing.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x1f, which jumps into the body of case 0x32, where AH of 0x1f takes the default drive whatever DL holds.
AL is 0xFF when the drive is out of range, not mounted or removable.
Get the DOS drive parameter block for a specific drive, a DOS 2 call.
DL is the drive number: 00h is the default, 01h is A:, and so on.
AL is 00h if successful.
On success DS:BX points to the Drive Parameter Block (DPB) of the specified drive.
AL is FFh for an invalid or network drive.
The call updates the DPB by reading the disk.
If disk access is not desirable, the DPB may be reached through the DOS list of lists.
The call was undocumented before DOS 5.0, and only the DOS 4.0 and later version of the DPB has been documented.
From offset 00h the DPB holds the drive number, unit number, bytes per sector, highest sector number in a cluster, cluster shift count, and at 06h the reserved sectors.
Then: FAT count, root entries, first data sector, highest cluster number (16-bit FAT if above 0FF6h, else 12-bit), sectors per FAT, first directory sector, driver header address.
It goes on with the media ID byte at 16h, 00h or FFh for disk accessed or not at 17h and the pointer to the next DPB at 18h.
Under DOS 2.x 1Ch is the cluster of the current directory and 1Eh the 64-byte ASCIZ pathname of that directory.
Under DOS 3.x 1Ch is the cluster where the free space search starts and 1Eh the number of free clusters, FFFFh if unknown.
Under DOS 4.0 to 6.0, 0Fh is a word of sectors per FAT, 11h the first directory sector and 13h the driver header address.
Under DOS 4.0 to 6.0, 17h is the media ID byte, 18h the disk accessed flag and 19h the pointer to the next DPB.
Under DOS 4.0 to 6.0, 1Dh is the cluster where the free space search starts, usually the last one allocated.
Under DOS 4.0 to 6.0, the DPB word at 1Fh is the number of free clusters on the drive, FFFFh if unknown.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x32, whose body the case 0x1f also reaches by its label.
AL is 0xFF when the drive is out of range, not mounted or removable.
When the word at offset 0x1F of the DPB is 0xFFFF, the free clusters from DOS_GetFreeDiskSpace32 are stored there.
Read a random record from an FCB file, a DOS 1 call.
DS:DX points to an opened FCB.
AL is 00h if the read succeeded.
AL is 01h at end of file, with no data read.
AL is 02h for a segment wrap in the DTA, with no data read.
AL is 03h at end of file when a partial record was read.
The Disk Transfer Area is filled with the record read from the file.
The record is read from the current file position as specified by the random record field of the FCB.
The record is read from the current file position as specified by the record size field of the FCB.
The file position is not updated after the record is read.
If a partial record is read, it is zero-padded to the full size.
